structure.title: Declaration · A list of injuries seeks an audience
structure.text: The colonies explain why a political bond can be dissolved. General propositions about rights open the case, but an extended indictment must then persuade readers that this king's conduct actually meets the threshold those propositions describe.

structure.title: Constitution · Turn a people into decision-making bodies
structure.text: The articles distribute offices, terms and powers among institutions. Following a bill, appointment or treaty through the relevant steps shows how many separate acts may be necessary before anyone can speak in the name of the whole.

structure.title: Bill of Rights · Put limits in writing
structure.text: The first ten amendments address speech, worship, searches, trial and the division of authority, among other matters. Each limit has an addressee. Paying attention to the actor being restrained gives a right a more precise political shape.

structure.title: Later amendments · Read the revisions against the originals
structure.text: Amendments abolish slavery, redefine citizenship, alter voting protections and revise machinery for elections and succession. The collection preserves the earlier language too, allowing a reader to see the particular settlement later generations decided to change.

people.name: The people
people.role: A claimed source of political authority
people.text: The phrase can authorise resistance in a declaration and establish offices in a constitution. Who could vote, count for representation or possess citizenship is a further question whose answer changes across the collection.

people.name: The states
people.role: Governments with a part in national decisions
people.text: States help constitute the Senate and ratify amendments. Following them across the articles reveals several different relationships between the states and the Union within what can sound like one simple division of powers.

context.title: These writings perform different acts
context.text: A declaration explains why its signers take an action. The Constitution creates an institutional order, while amendments change the text's operation. A powerful phrase in one document may have a different legal or rhetorical function in another.

notice.text: Look for slavery where the word itself is absent.
notice.why: Early provisions about counting persons, migration and persons held to service incorporate compromises in indirect language. Reading them beside the later prohibition makes the distance between two constitutional settlements concrete.

notice.text: Trace the verbs of a single appointment.
notice.why: Nominating, consenting and appointing can belong to different stages and actors. Institutional restraint is sometimes carried by the small space between verbs that sound nearly interchangeable in casual conversation.

opening: Declaring independence is one task; building a government strong enough to survive and restrained enough to trust is another. These documents move from the claim that people may replace oppressive rulers to the detailed allocation of powers, rights, and prohibitions. Their promises coexist with exclusions that later amendments confront. Read together, they show a republic being declared, constructed, and revised, with arguments over who counts among its people written into the words that generations would use to demand a place within it.
